evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.1.4: hōrā secundā calceōs poscit
terms.comment: A Roman hour was a twelfth of the time from sunrise to sunset, so it was longer in summer than in winter: hōra prīma was the first hour after sunrise, hōra sexta ended at noon and hōra duodecima at sunset; the night had twelve hours of its own, and midnight was sexta noctis hōra (Gell. 3.2.16). The modern way puts the same words on our clock (Traupman 80–81): prīma hōra is one o’clock, with ante merīdiem or post merīdiem where needed, and the Culīna Theodōrī counts the twenty-four hours (hōrā ūndēvīcēsimā, at 7 p.m.). So hōrā nōnā is 9 a.m. on our clock but mid-afternoon on the Roman one.

phrases.latin: māne lectulō continētur, hōrā secundā calceōs poscit, ambulat mīlia passuum tria
phrases.english: in the morning he stays in bed; at the second hour (the Roman way, counted from sunrise) he calls for his shoes and walks three miles
